name: False positive
seoDesc: False positive: work out prevalence from the specificity and the false positive. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: prevalence is what the False positive calculator works out, and it gets there from the specificity and the false positive. It is built for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the False positive calculator work?
sections.html:
The False positive calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports prevalence in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the specificity and the false positive.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the False positive calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Prevalence=(false positive + specificity − 1) ÷ (specificity − 1)
Prevalence=(specificity − true negative) ÷ specificity
False positive rate=1 − specificity

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Specificity = 10 % and False positive = 10 %. The calculator returns Prevalence = 88.8889 %, True negative = 1.1111 % and False positive rate = 90 %.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Prevalence = 88.8889 %, True negative = 1.1111 % and False positive rate = 90 % should be roughly the size you expected from Specificity = 10 % and False positive = 10 %.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The False positive calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the specificity and the false positive — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the False positive calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the False positive calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns prevalence, derived from the specificity and the false positive. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the False positive calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the specificity and the false positive, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter prevalence in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Prevalence opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Prevalence = 88.8889 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the False positive calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
